records.source: Κατ’ ἐκεῖνον δὲ τὸν καιρὸν ἐπέβαλεν Ἡρῴδης ὁ βασιλεὺς τὰς χεῖρας κακῶσαί τινας τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς ἐκκλησίας.
records.gloss: At that now the time put forth Herod the king the hands to mistreat some of those from the church.
pieces: At about that time King Herod moved against some of the church's people, meaning to do them harm.

L.1: Now at that time Herod the king laid [his] hands on some of those from the church to mistreat [them].

R.1: At that time King Herod began to attack some of the believers in the church. He wanted to hurt them.

decisions.choice: Herod the king: Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, king over Judea from AD 41 to 44
alternatives: Herod Antipas, who killed John the Baptist (Luke 9:9)
decisions.reason: Several rulers of the same family bore the name. Josephus tells how the emperor Claudius gave Agrippa I the whole of his grandfather's kingdom, Judea included (Antiquities 19.274-275), so that Jerusalem was ruled again by a Jewish king. His death, told in 12:20-23, fits the account Josephus gives of Agrippa I (Antiquities 19.343-350). Agrippa II, his son, is the king of 25:13-26:32.

decisions.choice: at that time: about the time of the famine relief of 11:27-30
decisions.reason: The phrase links the two stories loosely. Herod's death in AD 44 gives the latest date for the events of this chapter.

decisions.choice: laid hands on ... to mistreat: took action against them, to do them harm
alternatives: arrested them by his own hand
decisions.reason: To lay hands on someone is to seize or attack them (4:3, 5:18). The verb "to mistreat" says why.

decisions.choice: moved against
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the idiom in plain words.

decisions.choice: some of the believers in the church
alternatives: some of those from the church
decisions.reason: Readable says who the church's people were.

records.heading: Herod kills James and seizes Peter

records.source: ἀνεῖλεν δὲ Ἰάκωβον τὸν ἀδελφὸν Ἰωάννου μαχαίρῃ.
records.gloss: He killed then James the brother of John with [the] sword.
pieces: He executed James, John's brother, with the sword.

L.2: And he killed James the brother of John with [the] sword.

R.2: He gave orders to kill James, John's brother, with a sword.

decisions.choice: James the brother of John: James son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve
alternatives: James the brother of the Lord (12:17)
decisions.reason: James and John, the sons of Zebedee, were fishermen called by Jesus (Luke 5:10). Jesus told them they would drink the cup he drank (Mark 10:39). He is the first of the Twelve whose death Acts reports.

decisions.choice: with the sword: beheaded or run through, the way a ruler put people to death
decisions.reason: Death by the sword was a punishment carried out on a ruler's orders. The text gives no trial and no details.

decisions.choice: he killed: Herod had him killed
alternatives: Herod killed him with his own hand
decisions.reason: A ruler is said to do what he orders done.

decisions.choice: gave orders to kill
decisions.reason: Readable says how a king killed someone, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: ἰδὼν δὲ ὅτι ἀρεστόν ἐστιν τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις προσέθετο συλλαβεῖν καὶ Πέτρον ἦσαν δὲ ἡμέραι τῶν ἀζύμων, ὃν καὶ πιάσας ἔθετο εἰς φυλακήν, παραδοὺς τέσσαρσιν τετραδίοις στρατιωτῶν φυλάσσειν αὐτόν, βουλόμενος μετὰ τὸ πάσχα ἀναγαγεῖν αὐτὸν τῷ λαῷ.
records.gloss: Having seen now that pleasing it is to the Jews, he proceeded to arrest also Peter; were now [the] days of the Unleavened [Bread]; \v 4 whom also having seized he put in prison, having handed over to four squads of four soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring up him to the people.
pieces: When he saw how this pleased the Jews, he went further and had Peter taken too. It was the time of the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
Once Peter was seized, Herod put him in prison and handed him over to four squads of four soldiers to keep guard. His plan was to bring him out before the people when the Passover was over.

L.3: And having seen that it was pleasing to the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also (and these were the days of the Unleavened [Bread]),
L.4: and having seized him, he put [him] in prison, handing [him] over to four squads of four soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him up to the people.

R.3: Herod saw that this made the Jewish leaders and many of the people happy. So he arrested Peter too. This happened during the festival called the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
R.4: Herod put Peter in prison, and he gave him to sixteen soldiers to guard, four soldiers at a time. Herod planned to put Peter on trial in front of the people after the Passover festival.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the people of Jerusalem and their leaders who opposed the believers
decisions.reason: The believers themselves were Jews. Here the word names those in Jerusalem whom Herod wanted to please, as in 12:11; Josephus says Agrippa I took pains to win the favor of the Jews (Antiquities 19.330-331).

decisions.choice: the days of Unleavened Bread and the Passover: the spring festival, the Passover meal followed by seven days without yeast
decisions.reason: The two were kept together (Exodus 12:1-20; Luke 22:1), and "the Passover" could name the whole festival. Herod waits until it is over, perhaps so as not to hold a trial or execution during the feast. Jesus was arrested at the same festival (Luke 22:1-7).

decisions.choice: four squads of four soldiers: sixteen men taking turns, four for each watch of the night
decisions.reason: The night was divided into four watches; each squad of four took a watch. In 12:6 two soldiers are chained to Peter and two guard the door.

decisions.choice: to bring him up to the people: to bring him out for a public trial and sentence
alternatives: to set him free before them
decisions.reason: Herod meant to judge Peter in public, as Pilate brought Jesus out before the people (Luke 23:13-25). After James's death, a death sentence was likely; the text does not say.

decisions.choice: the note about the feast in parentheses
decisions.reason: The Greek breaks into the sentence to give the time; Literal shows the break with parentheses.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders and many of the people
decisions.reason: Readable says who "the Jews" were here, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: sixteen soldiers, four at a time; put Peter on trial in front of the people
alternatives: four squads of four soldiers; bring him up to the people
decisions.reason: Readable explains the squads and what bringing him to the people meant.

records.source: ὁ μὲν οὖν Πέτρος ἐτηρεῖτο ἐν τῇ φυλακῇ· προσευχὴ δὲ ἦν ἐκτενῶς γινομένη ὑπὸ τῆς ἐκκλησίας πρὸς τὸν θεὸν περὶ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: The indeed then Peter was being kept in the prison; prayer however was earnestly being made by the church to the God concerning him.
pieces: So Peter was under guard in the prison, but the church was praying to God for him without letup.

L.5: So Peter was being kept in the prison, but prayer was being made earnestly by the church to God for him.

R.5: So Peter was kept in prison. But the church did not stop praying to God for him. They prayed with all their hearts.

decisions.choice: earnestly: with intense effort, and without stopping
decisions.reason: The word means stretched out: intensely, and so steadily. Luke uses its relative of Jesus praying in the garden (Luke 22:44). The church was still praying when Peter arrived (12:12).

decisions.choice: on the one hand Peter was kept ... but prayer was made: two sides set against each other
decisions.reason: The Greek pairs the two clauses: the king's guard on one side, the church's prayer on the other.

decisions.choice: did not stop praying; with all their hearts
decisions.reason: Readable gives both sides of the word, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: Ὅτε δὲ ἤμελλεν προαγαγεῖν αὐτὸν ὁ Ἡρῴδης, τῇ νυκτὶ ἐκείνῃ ἦν ὁ Πέτρος κοιμώμενος μεταξὺ δύο στρατιωτῶν δεδεμένος ἁλύσεσιν δυσίν, φύλακές τε πρὸ τῆς θύρας ἐτήρουν τὴν φυλακήν.
records.gloss: When now was about to bring forth him Herod, the night that was Peter sleeping between two soldiers having been bound with chains two, guards also before the door were keeping the prison.
pieces: On the night before Herod was going to bring him out, Peter lay asleep between two soldiers, fastened with two chains, while guards in front of the door kept watch over the prison.

L.6: And when Herod was about to bring him forth, on that night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and guards before the door were keeping the prison.

R.6: Herod planned to bring Peter out to the people the next day. But that night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers. He was tied to them with two chains. Other soldiers were guarding the prison door.

decisions.choice: bound with two chains between two soldiers: chained to a guard on each side
decisions.reason: Romans sometimes chained a prisoner to the soldier who guarded him (28:16, 28:20). Peter is chained to two, a sign of how closely he was kept.

decisions.choice: sleeping: asleep, on what was to be his last night
decisions.reason: The verb means to sleep. Luke does not explain it, but Peter sleeps on the night before he was to be brought out, and the angel has to wake him (12:7).

decisions.choice: that night: the night before the day Herod had set
decisions.reason: The time clause says Herod was about to bring Peter out; it was that night.

decisions.choice: the next day
alternatives: when Herod was about to bring him forth
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly when Herod meant to act.

records.heading: An angel leads Peter out of prison

records.source: καὶ ἰδοὺ ἄγγελος κυρίου ἐπέστη, καὶ φῶς ἔλαμψεν ἐν τῷ οἰκήματι· πατάξας δὲ τὴν πλευρὰν τοῦ Πέτρου ἤγειρεν αὐτὸν λέγων· Ἀνάστα ἐν τάχει· καὶ ἐξέπεσαν αὐτοῦ αἱ ἁλύσεις ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν.
records.gloss: And behold, an angel of [the] Lord stood by, and a light shone in the cell; having struck then the side of Peter he raised him saying, Rise in haste. And fell off of him the chains from the hands.
pieces: All at once an angel of the Lord was standing there, and light filled the cell. He struck Peter's side and woke him: "Up, quickly!" And the chains dropped from his hands.

L.7: And look, an angel of [the] Lord stood by, and a light shone in the cell; and striking Peter's side, he woke him, saying, "Get up quickly." And his chains fell off his hands.

R.7: Suddenly an angel from the Lord was standing next to Peter, and a light shone in the prison room. The angel hit Peter on the side and woke him up. He said, "Get up! Hurry!" Right away the chains fell off Peter's wrists.

decisions.choice: an angel of the Lord: a messenger sent by God
decisions.reason: As in 5:19, where an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors for the apostles. Peter says afterward that the Lord sent his angel (12:11).

decisions.choice: striking: a firm blow to wake him
decisions.reason: The verb means to strike. Luke uses it again in 12:23, where an angel of the Lord strikes Herod: the same kind of messenger frees the apostle and judges the king.

decisions.choice: woke him: roused him from sleep
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to raise or to wake; Peter was asleep (12:6).

decisions.choice: all at once; suddenly
decisions.reason: The Greek word calls attention to a sudden event. Literal keeps it as "look".

decisions.choice: hit
decisions.reason: Readable uses the everyday word; the link with 12:23 is noted in the meaning note.

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ ὁ ἄγγελος πρὸς αὐτόν· Ζῶσαι καὶ ὑπόδησαι τὰ σανδάλιά σου· ἐποίησεν δὲ οὕτως.
records.gloss: Said then the angel to him, Gird yourself and tie on the sandals of you. He did then so.
pieces: The angel told him, "Fasten your belt and put your sandals on." Peter did as he was told.

L.8: Then the angel said to him, "Gird yourself and tie on your sandals." And he did so.

R.8: The angel said to him, "Put on your belt and your sandals." Peter did that.

decisions.choice: gird yourself: fasten the belt that held up the long tunic, ready to walk
decisions.reason: A man loosened his belt to sleep and tightened it to travel or work (Luke 12:35, 17:8). The Passover was to be eaten with belts fastened and sandals on (Exodus 12:11).

decisions.choice: belt and sandals at Passover time: a possible echo of Israel ready to leave Egypt
decisions.reason: The words of Exodus 12:11 are close, and the rescue comes in the Passover week (12:3-4). Luke does not draw the link himself.

decisions.choice: Peter
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Peter, since the angel has just spoken.

records.source: καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· Περιβαλοῦ τὸ ἱμάτιόν σου καὶ ἀκολούθει μοι.
records.gloss: And he says to him, Throw around the cloak of you and follow me.
pieces: Then he said, "Wrap yourself in your cloak and come after me."

L.8: And he says to him, "Throw your cloak around [you] and follow me."

R.8: Then the angel said, "Put on your coat and follow me."

decisions.choice: he says: the present tense in a story, making the scene vivid
decisions.reason: Greek storytellers often switch to the present tense for a lively moment. The speaker is still the angel.

decisions.choice: cloak: the outer garment worn over the tunic, used as a blanket at night
decisions.reason: Exodus 22:26-27 speaks of the cloak as a poor man's covering for the night.

decisions.choice: said
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the past tense, as English tells a story.

records.source: καὶ ἐξελθὼν ἠκολούθει, καὶ οὐκ ᾔδει ὅτι ἀληθές ἐστιν τὸ γινόμενον διὰ τοῦ ἀγγέλου, ἐδόκει δὲ ὅραμα βλέπειν.
records.gloss: And having gone out he was following, and not knew that real is what is happening through the angel; he was thinking however a vision to see.
pieces: So Peter went out and followed. He did not know that the things the angel was doing were real; he took it all for a vision.

L.9: And going out, he kept following, and he did not know that what was happening through the angel was real, but he thought he was seeing a vision.

R.9: Peter followed the angel out of the cell. But he did not know that this was really happening. He thought he was seeing a vision, like a dream.

decisions.choice: a vision: something God shows a person, not seen with the bodily eyes
decisions.reason: Peter had seen a vision in Joppa (10:10-17, 11:5). He thinks this is another such sight, until he comes to himself in 12:11.

decisions.choice: real: actually happening, not only seen
alternatives: true, as opposed to a lie
decisions.reason: The word means true; here it is set against a vision.

decisions.choice: like a dream
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word, as in 11:5.

records.source: διελθόντες δὲ πρώτην φυλακὴν καὶ δευτέραν ἦλθαν ἐπὶ τὴν πύλην τὴν σιδηρᾶν τὴν φέρουσαν εἰς τὴν πόλιν, ἥτις αὐτομάτη ἠνοίγη αὐτοῖς, καὶ ἐξελθόντες προῆλθον ῥύμην μίαν, καὶ εὐθέως ἀπέστη ὁ ἄγγελος ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Having passed through then a first guard and a second they came to the gate the iron the [one] leading into the city, which by itself was opened to them, and having gone out they went along street one, and immediately departed the angel from him.
pieces: They went past the first guard post and then the second, and came to the iron gate that opened onto the city. It swung open for them of its own accord. Out they went and on along one street, and suddenly the angel was gone from him.

L.10: And having passed through a first guard and a second, they came to the iron gate that leads into the city, which opened for them by itself; and going out, they went along one street, and at once the angel left him.

R.10: They walked past the first group of guards and then the second. Then they came to the iron gate that led out into the city. The gate opened for them by itself. They went out and walked to the end of a street. Then suddenly the angel left Peter.

decisions.choice: a first guard and a second: two guard posts inside the prison
decisions.reason: The word can mean a guard or a prison. Here it is one place of watch after another on the way out.

decisions.choice: opened by itself: God opened it
alternatives: the gate had been left unlocked
decisions.reason: The gate opening on its own is part of the wonder, as with the doors in 5:19 and 16:26.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "going out they went along one street"
alternatives: Codex Bezae adds "they went down the seven steps" before going along the street
decisions.reason: One Western manuscript, Codex Bezae, adds that they went down the seven steps, a detail that may come from local knowledge of the place. The SBLGNT does not include it. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: guard post
decisions.reason: Balanced says what kind of guard is meant, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἐν ἑαυτῷ γενόμενος εἶπεν· Νῦν οἶδα ἀληθῶς ὅτι ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ κύριος τὸν ἄγγελον αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐξείλατό με ἐκ χειρὸς Ἡρῴδου καὶ πάσης τῆς προσδοκίας τοῦ λαοῦ τῶν Ἰουδαίων.
records.gloss: And Peter in himself having come said, Now I know truly that sent out the Lord the angel of him and delivered me out of [the] hand of Herod and all the expectation of the people of the Jews.
pieces: Then Peter came to himself. "Now I know for certain," he said, "that the Lord sent {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} angel and snatched me out of Herod's grasp and from all that the Jewish people were waiting to see."

L.11: And Peter, having come to himself, said, "Now I know truly that the Lord has sent {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} angel and rescued me out of [the] hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the people of the Jews."

R.11: Then Peter understood what had happened. He said, "Now I am sure that this is real. The Lord sent {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} angel to save me from Herod. The Jewish leaders and people were hoping to see me killed, but the Lord saved me from all that."

decisions.choice: having come to himself: becoming fully aware
decisions.reason: The phrase is used of someone coming to his senses (Luke 15:17). Peter no longer thinks he is seeing a vision (12:9).

decisions.choice: the Lord sent his angel and rescued me: words like those spoken of God's rescues in the Scriptures
decisions.reason: In the Greek of Daniel 3:28 the king says that God sent his angel and rescued his servants; compare Daniel 6:22 and Exodus 18:4.

decisions.choice: the expectation of the people of the Jews: what the Jewish people were waiting for, Peter's trial and death
decisions.reason: Herod had arrested Peter to please the people (12:3) and meant to bring him out to them after the feast (12:4).

decisions.choice: the hand of Herod: Herod's power
decisions.reason: As in 11:21, the hand stands for power.

decisions.choice: were hoping to see me killed
alternatives: the expectation of the people of the Jews
decisions.reason: Readable says what they were expecting. The text does not say "killed", but James had been killed (12:2) and Herod meant to bring Peter out to the people.

records.source: Συνιδών τε ἦλθεν ἐπὶ τὴν οἰκίαν τῆς Μαρίας τῆς μητρὸς Ἰωάννου τοῦ ἐπικαλουμένου Μάρκου, οὗ ἦσαν ἱκανοὶ συνηθροισμένοι καὶ προσευχόμενοι.
records.gloss: Having realized [it] also he came to the house of Mary the mother of John the [one] being called Mark, where were many having gathered together and praying.
pieces: When he had grasped this, he made his way to the home of Mary, mother of John whose other name was Mark. A good number of people had come together there and were praying.

L.12: And having realized [this], he came to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was called Mark, where many were gathered together and praying.

R.12: When Peter understood what had happened, he went to the house of Mary. She was the mother of John, who was also called Mark. Many believers had come together there, and they were praying.

decisions.choice: having realized: having taken in his situation
alternatives: having thought it over and decided
decisions.reason: The verb means to see clearly or to understand. It may also suggest that he thought about where to go.

decisions.choice: Mary, the mother of John Mark: a believer whose house was a meeting place for the church
decisions.reason: John Mark goes with Barnabas and Saul in 12:25 and 13:5, leaves them in 13:13, and later sails with Barnabas (15:37-39). Colossians 4:10 calls him Barnabas's cousin. The house had a gateway and a slave girl (12:13), so it was a house of some size.

decisions.choice: many were gathered and praying: still praying at night
alternatives: they had met only for this
decisions.reason: The perfect participle shows they had come together and were there; the present participle shows they were praying when Peter came. 12:5 says the church kept praying.

decisions.choice: many believers
decisions.reason: Readable says who were gathered.

records.heading: Rhoda at the gate

records.source: κρούσαντος δὲ αὐτοῦ τὴν θύραν τοῦ πυλῶνος προσῆλθε παιδίσκη ὑπακοῦσαι ὀνόματι Ῥόδη, καὶ ἐπιγνοῦσα τὴν φωνὴν τοῦ Πέτρου ἀπὸ τῆς χαρᾶς οὐκ ἤνοιξεν τὸν πυλῶνα, εἰσδραμοῦσα δὲ ἀπήγγειλεν ἑστάναι τὸν Πέτρον πρὸ τοῦ πυλῶνος.
records.gloss: Having knocked then he [at] the door of the gateway, came a slave girl to answer, by name Rhoda; \v 14 and having recognized the voice of Peter, from the joy not she opened the gate, having run in however she reported to be standing Peter before the gate.
pieces: He knocked at the door in the gateway, and a servant girl named Rhoda came to see who it was.
She knew Peter's voice, and in her joy she left the gate shut. She ran inside and told them that Peter was standing at the gate.

L.13: And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a slave girl named Rhoda came to answer;
L.14: and recognizing Peter's voice, from joy she did not open the gate, but running in, she reported that Peter was standing before the gate.

R.13: Peter knocked at the door of the outside gate. A young servant woman named Rhoda came to the door to see who was there.
R.14: She knew it was Peter's voice. She was so full of joy that she forgot to open the gate! She ran back inside and told everyone, "Peter is standing outside at the gate!"

decisions.choice: slave girl: a young woman who was a slave in the household
decisions.reason: The word means a young girl, and is used most often of female slaves (Luke 12:45, 22:56; Acts 16:16). Such a girl answered the door (John 18:16-17).

decisions.choice: the door of the gateway: the door in the entrance from the street into the courtyard
decisions.reason: Larger houses had a gateway leading from the street into an inner courtyard. Rhoda answers from inside the gate without opening it.

decisions.choice: to answer: to see who was knocking
decisions.reason: The verb means to listen and so to answer a knock at the door.

decisions.choice: from joy: so glad that she forgot to open
decisions.reason: Luke uses the same phrase in Luke 24:41, where the disciples could not believe for joy. Her gladness, not fear, kept the gate shut.

decisions.choice: her report as direct speech
alternatives: she reported that Peter was standing before the gate
decisions.reason: Readable gives Rhoda's report in her own words to keep the sentences simple.

decisions.choice: servant girl (B); young servant woman (R)
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it; the meaning decision (m1) keeps that the person was owned, and Literal keeps "slave".

records.source: οἱ δὲ πρὸς αὐτὴν εἶπαν· Μαίνῃ.
records.gloss: They then to her said, You are mad.
pieces: They said to her, "You have lost your mind!"

L.15: And they said to her, "You are mad."

R.15: The people said to her, "You are crazy!"

decisions.choice: you are mad: you are out of your mind
decisions.reason: The verb means to rave, to be out of one's senses. Festus says the same to Paul in 26:24.

decisions.choice: the people
decisions.reason: Readable says who answered.

records.source: ἡ δὲ διϊσχυρίζετο οὕτως ἔχειν.
records.gloss: She however was insisting thus to be.
pieces: But she held firmly that it was true.

L.15: But she kept insisting that it was so.

R.15: But she kept telling them that it was true.

decisions.choice: kept insisting: she would not give in
decisions.reason: The imperfect tense pictures her saying it again and again.

records.source: οἱ δὲ ἔλεγον· Ὁ ἄγγελός ἐστιν αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: They then were saying, The angel it is of him.
pieces: So they said, "It is his angel."

L.15: And they kept saying, "It is his angel."

R.15: Then they said, "It must be Peter's angel."

decisions.choice: his angel: an angel thought to watch over Peter, who could look and sound like him
alternatives: a human messenger sent by Peter
Peter's ghost, because he was already dead
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks of the angels of the little ones, who see the face of the Father (Matthew 18:10). Some Jews of the time believed a person had a guardian angel who might appear in his likeness. The text does not say whether they thought Peter was dead; Luke reports their words without saying whether the belief was right.

decisions.choice: they kept saying: they repeated it, against her insisting
decisions.reason: The imperfect tense matches hers in 12:15b: she kept insisting, and they kept saying it was his angel.

decisions.choice: it must be Peter's angel
decisions.reason: Readable names Peter and shows that they were guessing.

records.source: ὁ δὲ Πέτρος ἐπέμενεν κρούων· ἀνοίξαντες δὲ εἶδαν αὐτὸν καὶ ἐξέστησαν.
records.gloss: But Peter was continuing knocking; having opened then they saw him and were amazed.
pieces: Peter, though, did not stop knocking. They opened the gate, saw him, and were beside themselves.

L.16: But Peter kept on knocking; and having opened [the gate], they saw him and were amazed.

R.16: All this time Peter kept on knocking. At last they opened the gate. When they saw Peter, they were completely amazed.

decisions.choice: were amazed: were astonished, almost out of their minds
decisions.reason: The verb means to be beside oneself. The church had been praying for Peter, yet they could not believe he was at the gate.

decisions.choice: kept on knocking: he went on knocking all the while they argued
decisions.reason: The verb means to keep on, and the participle shows the knocking going on.

decisions.choice: were beside themselves
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture in the verb.

records.source: κατασείσας δὲ αὐτοῖς τῇ χειρὶ σιγᾶν διηγήσατο αὐτοῖς πῶς ὁ κύριος αὐτὸν ἐξήγαγεν ἐκ τῆς φυλακῆς, εἶπέν τε· Ἀπαγγείλατε Ἰακώβῳ καὶ τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ταῦτα.
records.gloss: Having motioned then to them with the hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord him brought out of the prison, said then, Report to James and to the brothers these things.
pieces: He waved his hand to hush them and told them how the Lord had led him out of the prison. "Let James and the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} know about this," he said.

L.17: And motioning to them with [his] hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison, and he said, "Report these things to James and to the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}."

R.17: Peter waved his hand to tell them to be quiet. Then he told them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. He said, "Tell James and the other believers about this."

decisions.choice: James: the brother of the Lord, a leader of the church in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: James son of Zebedee had been killed (12:2). This James leads the church in Jerusalem in 15:13 and 21:18; Paul calls him the Lord's brother and a pillar of the church (Galatians 1:19, 2:9).

decisions.choice: the brothers: the other believers, men and women
decisions.reason: As in 11:1 and 11:29, the word means the believers.

decisions.choice: the Lord had brought him out: Peter gives the rescue to the Lord
alternatives: the angel acting on its own
decisions.reason: Peter has said that the Lord sent his angel (12:11).

decisions.choice: brothers and sisters, with "brothers" as the alternative
decisions.reason: As the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: the other believers
decisions.reason: Readable says who the brothers were.

records.source: καὶ ἐξελθὼν ἐπορεύθη εἰς ἕτερον τόπον.
records.gloss: And having gone out he went to another place.
pieces: Then he departed and went somewhere else.

L.17: And going out, he went to another place.

R.17: Then he left the house and went to another place.

decisions.choice: another place: somewhere Luke does not name
decisions.reason: Luke does not say where Peter went. He is back in Jerusalem at the meeting of 15:7. Guesses about the place go beyond the text.

records.source: Γενομένης δὲ ἡμέρας ἦν τάραχος οὐκ ὀλίγος ἐν τοῖς στρατιώταις, τί ἄρα ὁ Πέτρος ἐγένετο.
records.gloss: Having come then day, there was disturbance no small among the soldiers [as to] what then of Peter had become.
pieces: At daybreak the soldiers were in great alarm: what had happened to Peter?

L.18: And when day came, there was no small disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.

R.18: In the morning the soldiers were very upset. They did not know what had happened to Peter.

decisions.choice: no small disturbance: a great uproar
decisions.reason: Luke often says "no small" to mean "very great" (15:2, 19:23, 27:20).

decisions.choice: the soldiers' alarm: guards answered for their prisoner, often with their own lives
decisions.reason: A guard who lost a prisoner could suffer the prisoner's punishment; compare the jailer in 16:27 and the soldiers' plan in 27:42. 12:19 shows what happened to these guards.

decisions.choice: in great alarm; very upset
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say the meaning of the idiom plainly; Literal keeps it.

records.source: Ἡρῴδης δὲ ἐπιζητήσας αὐτὸν καὶ μὴ εὑρὼν ἀνακρίνας τοὺς φύλακας ἐκέλευσεν ἀπαχθῆναι, καὶ κατελθὼν ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰουδαίας εἰς Καισάρειαν διέτριβεν.
records.gloss: Herod then having searched for him and not having found, having examined the guards he commanded [them] to be led away, and having gone down from the Judea to Caesarea he was staying.
pieces: Herod had a search made for him, and when Peter could not be found, he questioned the guards and ordered them led off to execution. Then he left Judea, went down to Caesarea, and spent time there.

L.19: And Herod, having searched for him and not found [him], examined the guards and commanded [them] to be led away; and going down from Judea to Caesarea, he stayed [there].

R.19: Herod had people search everywhere for Peter, but they could not find him. Herod questioned the guards. Then he ordered that they be taken away and killed. After that, Herod left Judea and went to the city of Caesarea, and he stayed there for some time.

decisions.choice: to be led away: to be taken off for execution
alternatives: to be taken off to prison
decisions.reason: The verb means to lead away, and in court it is used of taking a prisoner off to punishment (Luke 23:26). Given what guards who lost a prisoner faced (16:27, 27:42), execution is the likely sense, but the verb alone does not say so.

decisions.choice: examined: questioned them as in a hearing
decisions.reason: The verb is used of a judicial inquiry (4:9, 24:8).

decisions.choice: went down from Judea to Caesarea: to the coastal city where Roman rulers and Herod's family kept a residence
decisions.reason: Caesarea by the sea was the seat of government (23:33). Josephus places Agrippa I's death there (Antiquities 19.343).

decisions.choice: to execution; taken away and killed
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what being led away meant, as the meaning note explains. Literal keeps the bare verb.

records.source: Ἦν δὲ θυμομαχῶν Τυρίοις καὶ Σιδωνίοις· ὁμοθυμαδὸν δὲ παρῆσαν πρὸς αὐτόν, καὶ πείσαντες Βλάστον τὸν ἐπὶ τοῦ κοιτῶνος τοῦ βασιλέως ᾐτοῦντο εἰρήνην διὰ τὸ τρέφεσθαι αὐτῶν τὴν χώραν ἀπὸ τῆς βασιλικῆς.
records.gloss: He was now furiously angry with Tyrians and Sidonians; with one accord then they came to him, and having persuaded Blastus, the [one] over the bedchamber of the king, they were asking peace, because was being fed their the country from the royal [country].
pieces: Herod had been in a bitter quarrel with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came to him together, and after winning over Blastus, the king's chamberlain, they sued for peace, for their land drew its food from the king's lands.

L.20: Now he was furiously angry with [the] people of Tyre and Sidon; and they came to him with one accord, and having won over Blastus, the [one] over the king's bedchamber, they asked for peace, because their country was fed from the king's [country].

R.20: Herod was very angry with the people of the cities of Tyre and Sidon. So these people came together to meet with him. First they made friends with Blastus, an important servant who took care of the king's private rooms. Then they asked Herod to make peace with them. They needed peace because their land got its food from the land Herod ruled.

decisions.choice: furiously angry: in a bitter quarrel, perhaps close to open conflict
decisions.reason: The verb means to fight with fury. Herod had no war with them, but his anger threatened their food supply.

decisions.choice: Tyre and Sidon fed from the king's country: the Phoenician coast depended on grain from Galilee and the land behind it
alternatives: they traded only in luxury goods
decisions.reason: The coastal cities had little farmland. Already in Solomon's day Tyre received wheat and oil from Israel (1 Kings 5:11), and Ezekiel 27:17 lists Judah and Israel among Tyre's suppliers of wheat.

decisions.choice: Blastus, over the king's bedchamber: the king's chamberlain, a trusted officer of the household
alternatives: a servant who only made the beds
decisions.reason: Such an officer had the king's ear. "Having persuaded" may mean they won him over with gifts; the text does not say how.

decisions.choice: peace: an end to the quarrel, with trade restored
decisions.reason: Here the word means good relations between peoples, as in Luke 14:32.

decisions.choice: chamberlain
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the English title of such an officer.

decisions.choice: an important servant who took care of the king's private rooms; asked Herod to make peace with them
alternatives: the one over the king's bedchamber; asked for peace
decisions.reason: Readable explains the title and says whom they asked.

records.heading: The death of Herod

records.source: τακτῇ δὲ ἡμέρᾳ ὁ Ἡρῴδης ἐνδυσάμενος ἐσθῆτα βασιλικὴν καὶ καθίσας ἐπὶ τοῦ βήματος ἐδημηγόρει πρὸς αὐτούς·
records.gloss: On an appointed then day Herod having put on clothing royal and having sat on the judgment seat was making a speech to them.
pieces: On the day that was set, Herod dressed in his royal robes, took his seat on the platform, and began to address them.

L.21: And on an appointed day Herod, having put on royal clothing and having sat on the judgment seat, was making a public speech to them.

R.21: On the chosen day Herod put on his royal clothes. He sat on his high seat and gave a speech to the people.

decisions.choice: the appointed day: a public occasion in Caesarea, which Josephus also describes
alternatives: a private meeting with the men of Tyre and Sidon
decisions.reason: Josephus tells of Agrippa I at a festival in Caesarea in honor of the emperor. At daybreak he came into the theater wearing a robe woven of silver that shone in the sun, and flatterers hailed him as a god (Antiquities 19.343-346). Luke and Josephus tell the same event in their own ways.

decisions.choice: judgment seat: a raised platform from which a ruler judged or spoke
decisions.reason: The same word is used for Pilate's and Gallio's seats (18:12; John 19:13).

decisions.choice: was making a public speech: addressing an assembled crowd
decisions.reason: The verb is used of speaking to a popular assembly. "To them" takes in the crowd, among them the men of Tyre and Sidon.

decisions.choice: platform; high seat
decisions.reason: Here Herod speaks rather than judges, so Balanced and Readable describe the seat.

records.source: ὁ δὲ δῆμος ἐπεφώνει· Θεοῦ φωνὴ καὶ οὐκ ἀνθρώπου.
records.gloss: The then people were crying out, Of a god a voice and not of a human!
pieces: The crowd kept shouting, "A god is speaking, not a human being!"

L.22: And the people kept crying out, "[The] voice of a god and not of {{gender:a human|a man}}!"

R.22: The people kept shouting, "This is the voice of a god! It is not the voice of a human!"

decisions.choice: a god: a divine being, as pagans spoke of their gods
decisions.reason: Without the article, and on the lips of a pagan crowd, the word means a god. Herod is honored as divine (compare 14:11, 28:6).

decisions.choice: a human: a mortal being, set against a god
decisions.reason: The word means a human being. The contrast is between divine and mortal.

decisions.choice: kept crying out: shouting again and again
decisions.reason: The imperfect tense pictures repeated shouting.

decisions.choice: a human, with "a man" as the alternative
decisions.reason: The word means a human being, as the meaning note explains; Balanced and Readable use an inclusive word with no setting.

records.source: παραχρῆμα δὲ ἐπάταξεν αὐτὸν ἄγγελος κυρίου ἀνθ’ ὧν οὐκ ἔδωκεν τὴν δόξαν τῷ θεῷ, καὶ γενόμενος σκωληκόβρωτος ἐξέψυξεν.
records.gloss: Immediately then struck him an angel of [the] Lord because not he gave the glory to the God, and having become eaten by worms he breathed his last.
pieces: At once an angel of the Lord struck him, since he had not given the glory to God; worms ate at him, and he died.

L.23: And immediately an angel of [the] Lord struck him, because he did not give the glory to God, and having become eaten by worms, he breathed his last.

R.23: Right away an angel from the Lord made Herod sick, because Herod did not give the glory to God. Worms ate his body, and he died.

decisions.choice: struck: an angel struck him with sickness
decisions.reason: The same verb is used in 12:7 for the angel waking Peter. Herod was struck at once; he died after being eaten by worms. Josephus says Agrippa I was seized by violent pains in the belly at that moment and died five days later (Antiquities 19.346-350).

decisions.choice: because he did not give the glory to God: he accepted the honor that belongs to God alone
decisions.reason: Luke gives the reason in so many words. Compare Isaiah 42:8 and Daniel 4:30-37, where a proud king learns that the Most High rules. Paul and Barnabas, hailed as gods, refuse the honor (14:14-15).

decisions.choice: eaten by worms: a disease that was seen as the death of a proud tyrant
decisions.reason: The participle comes before "breathed his last": the worms came before his death. A similar death is told of the persecuting king Antiochus IV (2 Maccabees 9:9).

decisions.choice: made Herod sick
decisions.reason: Readable says what the blow was, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: Ὁ δὲ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ηὔξανεν καὶ ἐπληθύνετο.
records.gloss: The but word of the God was growing and multiplying.
pieces: But the word of God went on growing and spreading.

L.24: But the word of God kept growing and multiplying.

R.24: But more and more people heard God's message and believed it.

decisions.choice: the word of God kept growing: the message spread and the believers increased, while the persecutor died
decisions.reason: The "but" sets the word against Herod. Luke gives similar summaries in 6:7 and 19:20; in 6:7 the same verbs are used of the word and of the disciples.

decisions.choice: more and more people heard God's message and believed it
alternatives: the word of God kept growing and multiplying
decisions.reason: Readable says what the growing of the word meant: more people heard and believed.

records.source: Βαρναβᾶς δὲ καὶ Σαῦλος ὑπέστρεψαν, εἰς Ἰερουσαλὴμ πληρώσαντες τὴν διακονίαν, συμπαραλαβόντες Ἰωάννην τὸν ἐπικληθέντα Μᾶρκον.
records.gloss: Barnabas then and Saul returned to Jerusalem having fulfilled the service, having taken along John the [one] having been called Mark.
pieces: Barnabas and Saul, once they had completed their service in Jerusalem, returned and took John, also called Mark, along with them.

L.25: And Barnabas and Saul returned, having fulfilled the service at Jerusalem, taking along with [them] John, who was called Mark.

R.25: Barnabas and Saul finished their work in Jerusalem. They had brought the gift there. Then they went back to Antioch. They took John Mark with them.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "to Jerusalem"
alternatives: many manuscripts read "from Jerusalem", with one of two Greek prepositions for "from"
some manuscripts read "from Jerusalem to Antioch"
decisions.reason: The manuscripts are divided. Several early ones read "to Jerusalem", the harder reading, since Barnabas and Saul were already in Jerusalem (11:30) and are back in Antioch in 13:1. Others read "from Jerusalem", which fits the story easily, and that ease may be why copyists changed it. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: "in Jerusalem" goes with the service: they returned after finishing their service in Jerusalem
alternatives: they returned to Antioch with no place given
decisions.reason: With the SBLGNT's wording, "to Jerusalem" can be read with "having fulfilled the service". Luke sometimes uses this preposition where "in" is meant (8:40, where Philip was found "at" Azotus). This reading fits the story: they had taken the gift to Jerusalem (11:29-30), and in 13:1 they are in Antioch. Read as "returned to Jerusalem", the sentence would describe a journey the story does not explain.

decisions.choice: the service: taking the famine gift to Judea
decisions.reason: The same word is used in 11:29 for the help the disciples sent.

decisions.choice: John called Mark: the son of Mary, in whose house the church met (12:12)
decisions.reason: He goes with them as their helper in 13:5.

decisions.choice: returned, having fulfilled the service at Jerusalem
alternatives: returned to Jerusalem, having fulfilled the service
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced place "Jerusalem" with the service, as the grammar note reads it. Literal says "at", a sense the preposition can bear, rather than "to".

decisions.choice: they had brought the gift there; they went back to Antioch
decisions.reason: Readable says what the service was and where they returned, from 11:29-30 and 13:1.
